Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
I feel like an object, not like a person
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.explanation: 'Noticing Weapons' is a poor fit for the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is evidence of weapon-related assault or generalized violence cues; the rest of the profile centers on interpersonal abuse and nonspecific danger rather than weapon-focused threat monitoring, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma context.

'Inaction Guilt' is clinically questionable in this context because it implies self-blame for not doing more to stop the abuse, which is less coherent with an ongoing coercive partner-abuse formulation than appraisals centered on shame, powerlessness, betrayal, or worthlessness. It is not impossible, but paired with the rest of the profile it stands out as weakly aligned with the trauma narrative and node pattern.

vignette: Mr. Nguyen, a 51-year-old South Eastern Asian man, has been experiencing significant distress since his wife’s violent outburst over six months ago. Mr. Nguyen had always trusted her completely, but the event shattered that trust and left him feeling deeply violated. The night of the abuse was vivid in his memory; it began as an ordinary evening at home, but soon escalated into a terrifying ordeal when he found himself facing unpredictable violence from someone he loved. Since then, Mr. Nguyen feels extremely tired most days, both physically and emotionally drained. This exhaustion is often triggered by seemingly minor situations where he feels uncomfortable or unsteady, such as unpredictable work meetings or interactions with colleagues at the office. These triggers frequently lead him to feel as if he were in imminent danger, even when there’s no real threat present. The memory of that night persists in fragments, appearing suddenly and disappearing just as quickly. He often experiences these sudden pieces of the memory during moments of exhaustion or discomfort, reinforcing his sense of vulnerability. The memories also force their way into his mind at unpredictable times, causing him to lose focus on tasks at work and leading to a growing fear that he might be attacked again. Mr. Nguyen has come to believe that nothing good can happen to him anymore, as the experience left him feeling dehumanized and betrayed by someone he trusted deeply. These negative appraisals have created a cycle of distress where his fear of danger is perpetually heightened. For instance, when he feels tired or uncomfortable at work, these feelings quickly escalate into a sense that he must constantly check behind him to ensure no one is following. His job as a tax inspector has become increasingly difficult due to this ongoing vigilance. He frequently finds himself distracted by his constant need to monitor his surroundings and his own state of fatigue. This has led to mistakes at work, which in turn intensify his feelings of dehumanization and betrayal. Mr. Nguyen is certain that he is no longer seen as a competent professional but merely an object subjected to scrutiny. The unpredictable nature of the memories exacerbates these negative appraisals, making him feel like an outsider even in familiar settings. He has started to avoid social gatherings and family events, fearing that any small discomfort or exhaustion might trigger another episode. This avoidance only reinforces his sense of betrayal and the belief that nothing good will ever happen again. Mr. Nguyen’s current state is marked by a pervasive sense of fear and isolation. The combination of feeling unsafe unless he can see all directions around him and constantly looking behind to check for threats has made daily activities unbearable. He finally sought help after realizing how deeply this experience had affected his relationship with his wife, as well as his ability to function at work. What frightens Mr. Nguyen most is the possibility that he will never feel safe again and that others might view him merely as a victim rather than a capable individual. His greatest hope is to regain a sense of normalcy and control over his life, free from the constant fear and unpredictability that now dominate his days.
